A volcano plot is the workhorse of differential-expression analysis: log fold change on x,
statistical significance on y, and the interesting genes pushed to the top corners. Here we build
one in Python with [canvasxpress](https://pypi.org/project/canvasxpress/) — interactive (zoom,
hover, filter) and **reproducible**: the whole figure is one portable specification you can store
and re-render from Python, R or JavaScript.

## Install

```bash
pip install canvasxpress
```

## A differential-expression table

Swap this simulated block for your own results — the output of any DE pipeline works, as long as you
have a log fold change and a significance value per gene.

::: {#40ff1612 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 1000
genes   = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(n)]
logfc   = rng.normal(0, 0.8, n)
neglogp = -np.log10(rng.uniform(size=n) ** 1.5)   # stand-in for -log10(p-value)

df = pd.DataFrame({"logFC": logfc.round(3), "-log-pVal": neglogp.round(3)}, index=genes)

def classify(fc, p):
    if fc > 1 and p > 2:   return "Increased"
    if fc < -1 and p > 2:  return "Decreased"
    return "NoChange"

group = [classify(fc, p) for fc, p in zip(df["logFC"], df["-log-pVal"])]
fold  = (2 ** df["logFC"].abs()).round(2)
```
:::


## Build the spec

canvasxpress takes a `data` object (a value matrix plus annotations) and a `config`. We put the two
measurements as the variable's samples and carry the regulation call and fold change as variable
annotations (`z`).

::: {#f7f044e8 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook

data = {
    "y": {"vars": ["logFC", "-log-pVal"], "smps": genes,
          "data": [df["logFC"].tolist(), df["-log-pVal"].tolist()]},
    "z": {"Group": group, "FC": fold.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Scatter2D",
    "title": "Publication-ready volcano plot",
    "xAxis": ["logFC"], "yAxis": ["-log-pVal"],
    "xAxisTitle": "log2 fold change", "yAxisTitle": "-log10 p-value",
    "colorBy": "Group",
    "colorKey": {"Group": {"Increased": "rgba(197,27,38,0.75)",
                            "Decreased": "rgba(33,102,172,0.75)",
                            "NoChange":  "rgba(150,150,150,0.35)"}},
    "sizeBy": "FC", "sizes": [3, 6, 9, 12, 15],
    "showDecorations": True,
    "decorations": {"line": [
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": 1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "x": -1},
        {"color": "rgba(120,120,120,0.8)", "width": 1, "y": 1.301},
    ]},
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="volcano", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
CXNoteBook(cx).render()
```

The chart is interactive — hover a point for its gene and values, drag to zoom, filter by regulation
group in the toolbar. The dashed guides mark the ±1 log2FC and p = 0.05 cutoffs.

## Why "reproducible"

Everything above serializes to one JSON specification — the `data` and the `config`. That spec is
portable: the identical figure renders from the R (`canvasXpress`) and JavaScript packages, and it
can be validated against a published schema and re-rendered later, so a figure in a paper can be
regenerated and audited rather than just viewed.
